questions.stem: An insurance carrier's COO tells you in a kickoff call: "We want AI to triage incoming claims. Our competitors already do it. How soon can you start building?" No one has said what "triage" produces, who acts on it, or what a wrong decision costs. Before any design work, what should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Run structured discovery to pin down the decision being made, who acts on it, how success is measured, the cost of each error type, and constraints such as latency and compliance.
Build a quick prototype on the most capable available model so the COO can react to something concrete, then reverse-engineer the requirements and success criteria from that reaction.
Draft a multi-agent reference architecture covering intake, fraud checks, routing and appeals, so the scope looks credible enough to secure budget and headcount early.
Write a detailed system prompt describing good claims triage, then refine requirements based on how well the outputs match the COO's expectations.

questions.explanation: Discovery comes before design. Anthropic's guidance on success criteria says they must be **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant**, and its agent guidance says to start from the simplest solution that meets the need. Neither is possible until you know what decision is being automated, who consumes it, what an error costs and which constraints (latency, cost, compliance) apply. Those answers decide everything downstream: the pattern, the model tier, whether a human review gate is needed, and the SLA.

whyWrong.B: A prototype built before the goal is defined anchors stakeholders on a demo rather than on a requirement, and "most capable model" is a cost and latency decision made with no data.
whyWrong.C: This is over-engineering before the problem is understood. Multi-agent designs cost far more tokens and are justified only when the task needs them, which nobody knows yet.
whyWrong.D: Prompt iteration needs a target to iterate toward. Without agreed success criteria, "matches the COO's expectations" is subjective and keeps moving.

questions.mindset: Define the problem and how success is measured before choosing any technology.

questions.stem: During discovery for a contract-review assistant at a law firm, you have a limited interview slot with the practice-group lead. You want the answers that will most directly decide the architecture: synchronous calls versus the Message Batches API, and whether human review is mandatory. Which TWO discovery questions should you prioritize? Choose TWO.

options.text: Is a lawyer or downstream process waiting on each result, and how quickly does it need to arrive?
Which Claude model do you prefer, and have you used any AI drafting tools before?
Would you prefer a chat interface or a document sidebar for reviewing the findings?
What happens when the assistant misses a risky clause or flags a safe one, and who is accountable?
How many example contracts can you share so we can add them as few-shot examples in the prompt?

questions.explanation: Two facts drive the biggest architectural forks here. **Latency tolerance** (A) decides synchronous versus batch: the Batch API halves cost but can take up to 24 hours, so it only fits work where nobody is waiting. **Cost of each error type and accountability** (D) decides whether you need a mandatory human-review gate, confidence-based escalation, or neither. Both are discovery-stage questions about the business, not the technology.

whyWrong.B: Model preference is a design decision the architect makes from measured trade-offs. It is not a requirement to collect from a business stakeholder.
whyWrong.C: UI form factor matters later, but it changes neither the processing mode nor the review gate.
whyWrong.E: Example contracts are valuable, but mainly for building an eval set. Collecting them as few-shot material answers neither architectural fork.

questions.mindset: Ask the questions whose answers change the architecture: latency tolerance and the cost of being wrong.

questions.stem: A retailer wants Claude to classify customer emails into eight routing queues. The support director describes the emails as "short, in English, and about orders or returns." You are writing up discovery findings, and the build is scheduled to start next week. Which discovery step will MOST reliably prevent a surprise once the system meets production traffic?

options.text: Ask the support director to write two example emails for each queue, so the prompt has clear canonical cases and the build team has a target before work starts.
Pull a representative sample of real historical emails, edge cases included, check it against the director's description, and keep it as the seed of the eval set.
Ask the vendor sales team for benchmark scores of the candidate models on email classification, to confirm the task is feasible.
Schedule a second interview with the director to confirm the eight queue definitions, their boundaries and the hand-off rules in more detail before the build starts.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder descriptions of their own data are often wrong at the edges. Real samples show non-English messages, forwarded threads, attachments, empty bodies and ambiguous intents. Anthropic's eval guidance says test sets should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases. Sampling real data during discovery tests the requirement against reality *and* gives you the starting eval dataset for design and iteration.

whyWrong.A: Invented examples reflect the director's mental model, which is exactly the assumption that needs testing. They will miss the messy cases.
whyWrong.C: Generic benchmarks say nothing about this retailer's inputs or queue definitions, so they cannot reveal a mismatch in the data.
whyWrong.D: Clearer queue definitions help, but another interview repeats the same unchecked assumptions about what the emails actually look like.

questions.mindset: Check stakeholder claims about data against real samples, and turn those samples into your eval set.

questions.stem: Discovery for an automated customer-refund agent has produced a conflict. The compliance lead requires a human to approve every refund. The operations VP needs refunds resolved within two minutes, around the clock, with no added headcount. The project sponsor has asked you to "just pick the sensible option" so the design can start this week. What is the MOST appropriate way for the architect to proceed?

options.text: Design for the compliance requirement, since regulatory concerns outrank operational ones, and inform the operations VP in writing that the two-minute target cannot be met under this design.
Design for the operations target, and add a strong system-prompt instruction to refuse any refund that looks risky, so that per-refund human approval becomes unnecessary.
Document the conflict, present business-framed options such as risk-tiered approval (small refunds automated, larger ones sent to a human), and have the accountable owner decide.
Build two parallel prototypes, one fully automated and one fully human-reviewed, and let the stakeholders choose after seeing both running in production for a month on live refunds.

questions.explanation: Conflicting requirements are a discovery output, not something the architect resolves quietly. The defensible step is to **make the conflict explicit, quantify the options in business terms** (risk exposure, turnaround, cost) and get a decision from the person who owns the risk. A risk-tiered design is often the compromise, but the accountable owner must choose it and the decision should be recorded so it is not reopened later.

whyWrong.A: This may be the eventual answer, but the architect is making a business-risk decision alone. The operations requirement is not discussed, just dropped.
whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction is probabilistic guidance. If compliance requires approval, that control has to be a deterministic gate in the workflow, not a request to the model.
whyWrong.D: Building two systems doubles the cost and puts an unapproved fully-automated path into production before the compliance question has been settled.

questions.mindset: Surface conflicting requirements with business-framed options and let the accountable owner decide; don't resolve them silently.

questions.stem: A hospital's patient-portal team says their new message-routing assistant "needs to be accurate." You are turning that into a success criterion to sign off at the end of discovery. Which criterion is the BEST one to agree on?

options.text: The assistant should route messages accurately and with good clinical judgment, as assessed by the portal team's clinical leads during a four-week pilot.
The assistant should run on the most capable Claude model available, so that routing accuracy is as high as possible.
The assistant should use fewer than 2,000 output tokens per message on average, keeping routing fast and the monthly cost predictable for the portal team's budget owner.
On a held-out set of 1,000 real de-identified messages, at least 95% reach the correct queue and no more than 0.5% of urgent clinical messages are routed as non-urgent.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance says good success criteria are **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant**, and often multi-dimensional. Option D names the dataset, the metric, the threshold, and a separate stricter limit on the costliest error type (missing an urgent message). That makes it testable in an eval and later usable as a monitoring threshold.

whyWrong.A: "Accurately and with good judgment" cannot be measured, so there is no way to tell whether the pilot passed.
whyWrong.B: This picks an implementation, not an outcome. A bigger model doesn't define or guarantee any level of accuracy.
whyWrong.C: This is measurable but beside the point: it limits cost and length, not whether messages reach the right queue.

questions.mindset: Success criteria must be measurable, tied to real data, and stricter on the costliest error.

questions.stem: A media company's architecture uses the Message Batches API to summarize all newly ingested articles, cutting processing cost roughly in half. In a steering meeting, the editorial director asks for a contractual SLA that "breaking-news summaries are ready within five minutes of ingestion," and the sponsor wants you to agree on the spot. What should the architect do?

options.text: Accept the SLA, because most batches finish well under an hour and breaking-news volume is small enough that those batches will almost always come back within minutes of submission.
Accept the SLA, but submit breaking-news items in their own small batches every five minutes so they are processed ahead of the larger daily batch of routine content.
Decline the SLA, explain that batch processing is asynchronous, and suggest the editorial team accept next-day summaries for all content.
Explain that batches carry no completion-time guarantee, and propose synchronous calls for breaking news under the five-minute SLA, keeping routine content on batch.

questions.explanation: An SLA must be one the architecture can actually meet. The Message Batches API cuts cost by 50% but is asynchronous: most batches finish within an hour, yet there is **no completion-time guarantee**, and requests still unprocessed after 24 hours expire. A five-minute promise on that path cannot be honored. The best answer **splits by latency need**: synchronous calls for time-critical items, batch for bulk, and a separate SLA for each path, explained in business terms (a small cost increase on a small slice of traffic buys the speed the newsroom needs).

whyWrong.A: "Usually fast" is not an SLA. A contract based on typical rather than guaranteed completion time will be breached, and the architect will own the breach.
whyWrong.B: Smaller or more frequent batches are still asynchronous. The API offers no completion-time guarantee for any batch, and under load more requests simply expire at 24 hours, so the SLA is still unsupported.
whyWrong.C: This is honest but needlessly unhelpful. It discards a legitimate business need that a hybrid design meets at modest extra cost.

questions.mindset: Never promise an SLA the processing mode can't guarantee; route by latency need and give each path its own SLA.

questions.stem: After a pilot, a bank's operations manager escalates: the same loan-summary request run twice produced differently worded summaries, and she wants a guarantee that "identical inputs always give identical outputs." Downstream systems read only five fields (applicant ID, product, amount, risk band, next action), and the narrative is for human readers. What is the MOST effective response?

options.text: Agree which parts must be consistent (the five fields, enforced with structured outputs and a JSON schema) and which may vary (the narrative), and report field-level consistency from evals.
Promise identical outputs by setting temperature to zero on every request, and document that setting in the SLA as the technical control that delivers consistency.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling Claude to always phrase summaries in the same fixed structure, and back it with several few-shot example summaries in that exact wording.
Cache the first response for each distinct input and return it for every repeat request, so that any user who submits the same loan request sees exactly the same summary text.

questions.explanation: LLM output wording varies from run to run, and no sampling setting or prompt makes a generative model deterministic. The architect's job is to **reset the expectation to what the business actually needs**: consistent structured fields for the downstream systems. Structured outputs with a JSON schema guarantee the *shape* of those fields, and eval results show how consistent the *values* are. Variation in the human-readable narrative is then accepted openly rather than hidden. This turns an impossible guarantee into a measurable one.

whyWrong.B: Sampling parameters reduce variation but never guaranteed identical outputs, so the SLA would be written against a control that cannot deliver it. On current Claude models the point is moot: `temperature` is deprecated and non-default values are rejected with a 400 error.
whyWrong.C: Instructions and examples make phrasing more consistent but cannot guarantee it. This hides the variation instead of aligning the expectation, and the next differently worded summary reopens the escalation.
whyWrong.D: A cache meets the literal request but not the need. Repeat-identical loan requests are rare, two near-identical applications still get different wording, and any error in the first run is frozen and repeated forever. The false expectation that LLM output is deterministic is left uncorrected.

questions.mindset: Align expectations on what must be deterministic, enforce that part structurally, and accept the rest openly.

questions.stem: An insurer's executive sponsor wants the support-reply assistant's contract to say it is "99% accurate, guaranteed on every response." Your offline eval on 2,000 real tickets shows 96.8% acceptable replies, with failures clustered in policy-exception cases. What is the MOST defensible commitment for the architect to propose?

options.text: Agree to 99%, since the remaining gap is small and likely to close with further prompt tuning and a few more few-shot examples added before the launch date.
A service-level objective measured on an agreed eval set plus sampled live traffic, with policy exceptions routed to human agents and the target reviewed periodically.
Refuse any accuracy commitment, since generative model outputs are non-deterministic and a percentage measured on an offline set says nothing reliable about live traffic.
Commit to 99% by asking Claude to rate its confidence on each reply and automatically suppressing any reply it rates below 99% confident, routing those to an agent.

questions.explanation: A per-response guarantee is not something a probabilistic system can honestly offer. The architect should turn it into an **objective measured the same agreed way over time** (a fixed eval set plus sampled production traffic), state the known failure area openly, and **design around it** by routing policy exceptions to humans. That ties the commitment to evidence rather than hope.

whyWrong.A: Committing to a number above measured performance, on the hope that tuning closes the gap, is how SLA breaches and loss of trust happen.
whyWrong.C: Accuracy can be measured through evals and production sampling, and the offline number is the best estimate available. Refusing any commitment leaves the business with nothing to plan around.
whyWrong.D: Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated and is not a reliable gate. It also does not turn a measured 96.8% into a guaranteed 99%.

questions.mindset: Turn 'guaranteed accuracy' into a measured objective plus a design that handles known failure areas.

questions.stem: Three weeks after launching an internal HR-policy assistant, feedback arrives as anecdotes in a chat channel. Each time, an engineer edits the system prompt to fix the reported case. Last week's fix for parental-leave questions broke answers about relocation benefits, and stakeholders now say the assistant is "getting worse." What change will MOST effectively restore a reliable feedback loop?

options.text: Have Claude review its own answer for policy accuracy before replying, so that errors are caught before users see them and fewer complaints reach the chat channel.
Move to a larger, more capable model so that each prompt edit is less likely to break unrelated behavior in other policy areas, and keep the current process.
Capture feedback in a structured form, triage it, add each confirmed failure to a regression eval set, and require every prompt change to pass the full set before release.
Hold a weekly meeting with HR stakeholders to review the anecdotes together and agree which prompt edits to make before the next release goes out.

questions.explanation: The root cause is **change without regression testing**. The loop works when feedback becomes data: structured capture, triage, conversion of each confirmed failure into an eval case, and a gate that blocks releases that regress earlier cases. Anthropic's eval guidance favors automated, task-specific test sets, so each fix leaves a permanent test behind.

whyWrong.A: Self-checking may catch some errors, but it adds latency and does nothing about the actual failure: untested prompt edits causing regressions.
whyWrong.B: A bigger model does not remove the need to test changes. Unrelated regressions can still happen, and nobody would know until users complain.
whyWrong.D: Meetings improve communication but leave the process unchanged. Edits would still ship without a check that previous fixes still hold.

questions.mindset: Turn every piece of feedback into a regression test, and gate changes on the full suite.

questions.stem: You are about to launch a pilot of a procurement-question assistant for a manufacturer's buyers. The sponsor has seen only polished demos. Which TWO actions will MOST improve expectation alignment before the pilot goes live? Choose TWO.

options.text: Tell users the assistant will learn from their conversations during the pilot, so its accuracy will improve on its own week by week.
Share the eval results with stakeholders: the measured success rate, the known failure categories and the cases the assistant is designed to hand to humans.
Use the best-case response times from the demos as the latency SLA, to keep the sponsor's enthusiasm high going into the pilot.
Hold back the known limitations until the pilot ends, so early users form an unbiased impression of the assistant and feedback is not primed by a list of caveats.
Agree the feedback channel, triage owner, review cadence and the criteria that decide whether the pilot expands, before launch.

questions.explanation: Expectation alignment means **showing evidence and agreeing the process in advance**. Sharing measured performance and known limitations (B) replaces impressions from the demo with data. Agreeing the feedback channel, owners, cadence and expansion criteria up front (E) means pilot results are judged against terms both sides accepted, not renegotiated afterwards.

whyWrong.A: Claude does not update its weights from your API conversations. Any improvement comes from your own changes to prompts, retrieval or design, so this sets a false expectation.
whyWrong.C: Demo latency is a best case. SLAs should come from measurements under production-like conditions, or they will be broken.
whyWrong.D: Hiding limitations guarantees a trust problem when users run into them, and it damages the feedback the pilot is supposed to produce.

questions.mindset: Show the evidence, including limitations, and agree how success will be judged before launch.

questions.stem: A sales-enablement assistant answers rep questions by calling two internal tools and then writing a response. In demos it replied in about 3 seconds. In a production-like load test, median end-to-end time is 6 seconds and p95 is 14 seconds, mostly from long answers and tool round-trips. The sponsor wants a latency SLA in the contract this month. Which SLA proposal is MOST appropriate?

options.text: An SLA of 3 seconds average, matching the demo, plus an action plan to tune the prompt and shorten answers until production performance matches the demo.
"Responses as fast as technically possible," since tool latency depends on internal systems the architect does not control and cannot commit on behalf of.
A hard cap on total response time enforced by setting a small max_tokens value on every call, so that no answer can run longer than the target regardless of load.
p50 and p95 targets for end-to-end time and for time-to-first-token of the streamed answer, measured on production traffic and based on the load-test baseline.

questions.explanation: Latency SLAs should use **percentiles on the real end-to-end path**, measured the same agreed way, not averages from a demo. Anthropic's latency guidance separates total latency from time-to-first-token and notes that streaming improves perceived responsiveness. Basing the targets on the load-test numbers keeps the promise achievable, and stating the measurement window makes it auditable.

whyWrong.A: A target taken from best-case demo numbers is already broken by measured data. An average also hides the slow tail that users notice.
whyWrong.B: This cannot be measured or enforced, so it gives the business nothing to plan around and cannot be checked.
whyWrong.C: max_tokens is a blunt cap that truncates answers mid-thought. It limits output length, not tool round-trip time, and can damage quality.

questions.mindset: Define latency SLAs as measured percentiles on the real path, using a production-like baseline.

questions.stem: A document-extraction system has run in production for a year on one pinned Claude model. Anthropic has emailed that the model is deprecated and will be retired in about two months, and has named a recommended replacement. The product owner asks for the update "with minimal risk." What should the architect do?

options.text: Run the existing eval suite on the replacement, compare quality, latency and cost with the current baseline, fix regressions, then roll out in stages before retirement.
Change the model ID in configuration on the retirement date, since the recommended replacement is newer and should perform at least as well on every task the system currently handles.
Keep the current model until requests start failing, since a working production system should not be changed before it has to be.
Rewrite the prompts from scratch for the new model before switching, since prompts tuned for an older model should not be assumed to carry over to a newer one.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's deprecation guidance says to test applications with replacement models **well before** the retirement date (customers get at least 60 days' notice), because requests to retired models fail. The lifecycle answer is to treat a model change like any other release: re-run the evals, compare against the baseline, fix regressions, and roll out in stages. This is the main reason an eval suite must be kept alive after handoff.

whyWrong.B: Newer does not mean better on your specific task. Waiting until the retirement date leaves no time to find and fix regressions.
whyWrong.C: Requests to a retired model fail, so waiting for failures turns a planned migration into a production outage.
whyWrong.D: Rewriting everything adds risk and work without evidence that it is needed. Run the evals first and change only what regresses; the migration guide may suggest adjustments, but they should be driven by measured gaps.

questions.mindset: Treat a model migration as a release: re-run the evals against the baseline, then roll out in stages.

questions.stem: Your team is handing a production claims-summarization system over to the client's internal platform team, who will run and evolve it after your engagement ends. Which TWO handoff deliverables are MOST important for the client to operate the system safely? Choose TWO.

options.text: A full export of the development chat history, so the client can trace how each prompt wording was reached.
A statement that the prompts are final and should not be edited, so the client team avoids introducing regressions.
A runbook covering the monitored signals and alert thresholds, common failure modes and their fixes, and escalation contacts.
A polished slide deck summarizing the architecture for the client's executive steering committee.
The eval suite and its baseline results, with instructions for running it before any prompt, model or retrieval change.

questions.explanation: Handoff succeeds when the receiving team can **detect problems** and **change the system without breaking it**. A runbook (C) covers detection and response. The eval suite with baselines and a documented regression procedure (E) makes future changes, including forced model migrations, safe. Together they move ownership of operations and iteration to the client.

whyWrong.A: Raw development transcripts are noise. Decisions should be captured in concise decision records, not chat logs.
whyWrong.B: Prompts will need to change (new policies, model retirements, input drift). Freezing them just pushes the risk to a later date and offers no safe way to make changes.
whyWrong.D: Executive summaries help with communication, but they give the operating team nothing to run or change the system with.

questions.mindset: Hand over the means to detect problems and the means to change safely: runbook plus evals.

questions.stem: A routing assistant for an e-commerce company has run for six months. Uptime is 99.95%, API error rates are flat, and user complaints are low. Last month the company launched a new home-services line, and agents in that queue say tickets are "landing in odd places," though complaint numbers have barely changed. Which monitoring addition would have detected this problem EARLIEST?

options.text: Alerts on API error rates and p95 latency broken down by queue, with a dashboard that the operations team reviews at the start of every shift.
Scheduled grading of a sample of production traffic against the eval rubric, plus tracking of how the incoming input mix shifts against the launch baseline.
An alert on weekly user-complaint volume per queue that fires when complaints rise more than 20% above the trailing six-month average.
Tracking of average input and output tokens per request by queue, with an alert when either moves outside its normal range for more than a day.

questions.explanation: This is **quality drift caused by a change in inputs**, and infrastructure metrics cannot see it: the system is up, fast and error-free while giving wrong answers. Detecting it early needs **quality monitoring**, meaning regular grading of sampled live traffic against the rubric (by code, an LLM judge or a human), plus watching the input distribution so that a new category of request shows up as a signal before outcomes degrade.

whyWrong.A: Errors and latency measure availability and speed. Wrong routing returns HTTP 200 quickly, so these alerts would stay silent.
whyWrong.C: Complaints arrive late and are incomplete. The scenario says they barely moved, so this alert would not have fired.
whyWrong.D: Token counts might shift slightly, but they do not measure correctness, so any alert would be noisy and indirect.

questions.mindset: Uptime is not quality: monitor graded output samples and shifts in the input mix.

questions.stem: A pilot of an invoice-coding assistant in one region scored 85% correct general-ledger codes against the 92% target agreed in discovery. The CFO is impressed with the time savings and wants to roll out to all twelve regions next month "and fix accuracy along the way." What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Proceed with the full rollout as the CFO asks, and monitor accuracy closely in every region so that problems can be fixed in production as they appear.
Redesign the system as a multi-agent pipeline with a dedicated reviewer agent before any rollout, since a single agent has missed the accuracy target.
Keep expansion gated on the agreed target: analyze the failed-code clusters, make targeted fixes, re-run the evals, then expand region by region once the target is met.
Revise the target down to 85% in the rollout plan, since the pilot shows this is the realistic level for the current design and the CFO is satisfied with the savings.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle phases exist so that **iteration happens before scale**. The exit criteria agreed in discovery are the gate, and the gap is a reason to iterate: group the failures, fix the causes, re-run the evals. A staged rollout meets the CFO's goal without taking on twelve regions' worth of miscoded invoices. Telling the CFO this in business terms (the cost of correcting miscodes at scale against a short delay) keeps the sponsor on board.

whyWrong.A: Rolling out multiplies the cost of errors twelvefold, and "fixing along the way" drops the agreed gate with no plan for what to fix.
whyWrong.B: This is over-engineering before diagnosis. The failure clusters may have simple causes such as missing reference data or unclear code definitions.
whyWrong.D: The architect would be resetting the agreed criterion to fit the result, with no diagnosis of whether 92% is reachable. If the business wants to accept more miscodes, that is a decision for the accountable owner, made with the cost of errors at twelve-region scale in front of them, and recorded.

questions.mindset: Expansion is gated on the agreed criteria; close the gap through targeted iteration, then scale in stages.

questions.stem: Looking back at a project that degraded quietly after handoff, your practice lead asks which discovery-phase outputs should be carried through every later phase (design, handoff, monitoring, iteration) so that the next engagement doesn't repeat the mistake. Which TWO outputs are MOST valuable to carry forward? Choose TWO.

options.text: The agreed success criteria and thresholds, reused as release gates during iteration and as alert thresholds in production monitoring.
The first prototype prompt, kept as the fixed specification that later prompt versions must not depart from.
Transcripts of the stakeholder interviews, summarized into the production system prompt so the model carries the full business context into every request.
The representative sample of real inputs and edge cases, grown into the regression eval set that each change and model migration must pass.
The original vendor comparison deck, reviewed at each phase to confirm that the chosen model remains the best option.

questions.explanation: Discovery outputs earn their value when they become **working parts of the system**. Success criteria (A) become eval gates and monitoring thresholds, so "good" means the same thing at launch and a year later. The real-input sample (D) becomes the regression suite that catches drift and makes model migrations safe. Without these, quality can drop quietly after handoff because nothing measures it against the original agreement.

whyWrong.B: Prompts should evolve as inputs, policies and models change. Freezing an early prototype prompt confuses one implementation with the requirement.
whyWrong.C: Interview material belongs in distilled requirements and decision records, not in the system prompt. Loading it there adds irrelevant tokens to every request and still measures nothing about whether the system meets the original agreement.
whyWrong.E: A static deck becomes outdated quickly. Model choices should be checked against your own evals, not an old comparison.

questions.mindset: Discovery outputs should become the eval gates and monitoring thresholds for the system's whole lifecycle.
